rationale: B wins because it cuts the deck into cleaner, more usable stories, especially the data angle: "Half the prep time: what a guacamole robot actually does to a lunch rush." A is strong, but it keeps two versions of the same causal-money story and lets the headline "Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices" put words in the company's mouth. B still overreaches in places, but it does a better job refusing duplicates and naming the proof a reporter would demand.
gaps_in_A: "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" overstates causality. The update says the robot rollout and price hold coexist; it does not prove one enables the other.
"Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices" is wrong attribution. Chipotle did not say robots justify the price decision, and that distinction matters.
"Its Competitors Are Taking Notes" invents competitor reaction. No competitor evidence was supplied.
The consumer price angle and investor margin angle both orbit the same unproven thesis: automation absorbing food-cost inflation. Different inbox, same skeleton.
gaps_in_B: "it's the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format" is an invented novelty claim. The update gives no first-mover evidence and no full-line automation proof.
"100 stores now, 3,500+ possible" quietly smuggles in a scale story. Only 100 restaurants are confirmed.
"Run the detector first" is not the obvious next step for a company-owned announcement. Pick the lead angle and fit-check real beat reporters first unless this is explicitly a newsjack.
"all four collapse into commentary" assumes uncertainty about authorization that was not in the brief. Useful warning, but too much of a side quest.
